title_en: Supreme People's Court Releases Three Typical Cases of Insurance Contract Disputes
keywords_en: contract dispute; insurance contract; court publishes three insurance contract disputes
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Publishes Three Typical Cases of Insurance Contract Disputes

Case 1:

Wang v. XX Life Insurance Co., Ltd. — dispute over a life insurance contract

—— Legal consequences of proxy signature on insurance contract

Key Points

An applicant for insurance should personally sign or seal when concluding an insurance contract. If an insurance agent signs on behalf of the applicant, but the applicant has already paid the insurance premium, it is deemed to be ratification of the proxy signature.

Provisions involved in Interpretation (II): Paragraph 1 of Article 3. If the applicant or the applicant's agent fails to personally sign or seal when concluding an insurance contract, and the insurer or the insurer's agent signs or seals on their behalf, the contract shall not become effective against the applicant. However, if the applicant has already paid the insurance premium, it is deemed to be ratification of the proxy signature or seal.

Brief Facts

Zhang, an insurance agent of the insurance company, and Wang, the applicant for insurance, were former classmates. When Zhang was promoting insurance products to Wang, Wang was on a business trip out of town. Wang then asked Zhang to go to his home to collect the insurance premium from his wife. Zhang went to Wang's home, obtained the insurance premium from Wang's wife, and signed Wang's name on the application form. The application form recorded both the applicant and the insured as Wang. The type of insurance purchased was critical illness insurance, with a lifetime insurance period, a premium payment period of 20 years, and an annual premium of RMB 2,000. After Wang returned to Beijing from his business trip, Zhang delivered the insurance contract and the premium invoice to Wang. Thereafter, Wang paid the annual premiums on time, totaling RMB 12,000. In 2006, after the relationship between Wang and Zhang deteriorated, Wang sued the insurance company, demanding a refund of all premiums on the ground that the application form was not signed by him personally.

Court Judgment

The court held that after Zhang signed the application form on Wang's behalf, Wang received the insurance contract text and the premium invoice delivered by Zhang, which should be deemed as Wang having knowledge of the proxy signing act carried out by Zhang. In the subsequent five years, Wang's act of paying the annual premiums in full and on time in accordance with the insurance contract constituted an expression of ratification of Zhang's proxy signing act through active participation in the performance of the contract. Accordingly, the court found that Wang had ratified Zhang's act of concluding the insurance contract on his behalf and rejected Wang's claims.

Case 2:

Tian and Ran v. XX Insurance Company — dispute over a life insurance contract

—— Rescission of insurance contract and insurer's refusal to compensate

Key Points

If the insurer fails to rescind the contract within the statutory period, it loses the right to rescind the insurance contract. If the insurer refuses to compensate on the ground that the applicant breached the duty of utmost good faith, the people's court shall not support such refusal.

Provisions involved in Interpretation (II): Article 8. If the insurer, without exercising the right to rescind the contract, directly refuses to compensate on the ground that the circumstances provided in paragraphs 4 and 5 of Article 16 of the Insurance Law exist, the people's court shall not support such refusal, unless the parties otherwise reach an agreement on the matter of refusal to compensate and the continuation of the insurance contract.

Brief Facts

Xiao Tian was the son of Tian and Ran. On June 21, 2007, Tian concluded an insurance contract with an insurance company. The contract provided that the applicant was Tian, the insured was Xiao Tian, the insurance beneficiaries were Tian and Ran, the type of insurance was whole life insurance, the insurance period was lifetime, the sum insured was RMB 20,000, and if the insured died, the insurance company would pay a death benefit equal to three times the basic sum insured. After the contract was concluded, Tian paid the premiums for 2007 to 2009 totaling RMB 4,500 to the insurance company on time in accordance with the contract. On November 23, 2009, the insured, Xiao Tian, died of tuberculosis. Tian, believing this to be an insured event, applied to the insurance company for compensation. On December 25, 2009, the insurance company issued a Notice of Refusal to Pay Insurance Benefits to Tian, which stated, "...after investigation, we found that the insured had suffered from a disease prior to applying for insurance. According to relevant legal provisions and the terms of the insurance contract,...this accident is not covered by the insurance liability of this company....This contract is terminated,...and the cash value of the policy, RMB 2,116.74, will be refunded...." Tian and Ran then filed a lawsuit, demanding that the insurance company jointly pay insurance benefits of RMB 60,000. It was also found that Xiao Tian had received diagnosis and treatment for tuberculosis in 2001 and 2008. On June 19, 2007, when Tian applied for insurance, in completing item 7(c) of the personal insurance application form: "Has the insured ever suffered from or received treatment for asthma, tuberculosis, emphysema,...or other diseases?", both the applicant Tian and the insured Xiao Tian answered "No."

Court Judgment

The court held that Tian failed to fulfill the duty of utmost good faith to the insurance company regarding the fact that the insured Xiao Tian had suffered from "tuberculosis" at the time of application, and the insurance company had the right to rescind the contract. Based on the facts of the case, the insurance company issued the Notice of Refusal to Pay Insurance Benefits on December 25, 2009. The content of this notice confirmed that the insurance company should have known of the grounds for rescission as of December 25, 2009. However, the insurance company did not exercise the right to rescission within 30 days from the date it knew of the grounds, and its right to rescission was extinguished. Since the insurance contract involved in this case had not been rescinded, it remained binding on both parties. The insurance company should bear the responsibility of paying insurance benefits to Tian and others in accordance with the provisions of the insurance contract. The judgment set aside the original civil judgment of the first instance and ordered the insurance company to bear the insurance liability.

Case 3:

Wu v. XX Insurance Company — dispute over a property insurance contract

—— Scope of "clauses that exempt the insurer from liability"

Key Points

In the standard form contract provided by the insurer, clauses on liability exemption, deductible rates, and proportional payment may be deemed as "clauses that exempt the insurer from liability" as stipulated in paragraph 2 of Article 17 of the Insurance Law, and the insurer shall fulfill the duty of prompt and clear explanation.

Provisions involved in Interpretation (II): Article 9. Clauses in the standard form contract provided by the insurer that exempt or reduce the insurer's liability, such as liability exemption clauses, deductibles, deductible rates, proportional payment or benefits, may be deemed as "clauses that exempt the insurer from liability" as stipulated in paragraph 2 of Article 17 of the Insurance Law. Clauses that grant the insurer the right to rescind the contract due to the applicant's or insured's breach of statutory or contractual obligations are not "clauses that exempt the insurer from liability" as stipulated in paragraph 2 of Article 17 of the Insurance Law.

Brief Facts

On November 17, 2004, Wu insured his car with an insurance company for vehicle damage insurance, a special clause waiving the deductible for main risks, occupant liability insurance, etc. The insurance contract stated: 1. Family self-use automobile loss insurance clauses. Paragraph 8 of Article 12 stipulated that the insurance company would not compensate for any losses or expenses incurred during any period when the insured vehicle was used for commercial activities for profit. 2. Motor vehicle third-party liability insurance clauses. Article 32 stipulated that the insurance company would bear corresponding compensation liability according to the proportion of liability borne by the driver of the insured vehicle in the accident, and would deduct at the agreed deductible rate within the liability limit stated in the insurance policy. If multiple claims occurred within the same insurance year, the deductible rate would increase by 5% starting from the second claim. If an insured accident occurred when a non-operating vehicle was engaged in commercial transport activities, causing losses to a third party, compensation would be calculated based on the ratio of the premium for this insurance to the premium for the corresponding commercial vehicle. 3. Additional insurance clauses and interpretations. It stated that occupant liability insurance was an additional insurance to third-party liability insurance. Paragraph 3 of Article 4 of the occupant liability insurance clauses stipulated that an absolute deductible rate of 20% applied to each compensation. On May 31, 2005, Wu drove the insured vehicle and collided with a tractor driven by a third party Hu, causing damage to the vehicle and injuries to Wu and passengers Yu and Lu. The traffic police brigade issued a traffic accident determination, finding Wu and Hu equally liable. According to a court judgment, Yu's losses totaled RMB 28,887, and Lu's losses totaled RMB 955.30, with Hu and Wu bearing joint and several liability for these losses. Wu applied to the insurance company for compensation. The insurance company argued that Wu had used the vehicle for commercial profit, which, according to the insurance clauses, exempted the insurance company from liability. Regarding the losses of Yu and Lu, the insurance company agreed to pay compensation based on the proportion stipulated in the insurance clauses. Wu argued that when concluding the insurance contract, the insurance company did not deliver the insurance clauses or provide the necessary explanation and clarification regarding the liability exemption clauses on which the insurance company relied for refusing compensation and paying proportionally. Wu filed a lawsuit, demanding that the insurance company compensate all losses.

Court Judgment

The court held that the issue in dispute was whether the deductible events and deductible rates stipulated in the insurance clauses provided by the insurance company constituted liability exemption clauses and whether such clauses became effective. In this case, the provisions in the insurance clauses provided by the insurance company regarding the exemption of the insurer's liability should be deemed as "clauses that exempt the insurer from liability" as stipulated in the Insurance Law, and the insurer should fulfill the duty of clear explanation with respect to these clauses.
